Lecture 21

Meromorphic functions, gamma continuation and residue sums

We prove that continuation along a path is unique, define meromorphic functions and show that a meromorphic continuation with poles in a suitable set is unique. A function already analytic on the plane minus its poles continues along every path without a choice, in contrast to the logarithm of Lecture 16. We prove that the gamma integral is analytic on the right half-plane, continue it to a meromorphic function on C\CC, and compute the residues at its poles. Finally, we sum series over the integers with the auxiliary functions πcot⁡(πz)\pi\cot(\pi z)πcot(πz) and π/sin⁡(πz)\pi/\sin(\pi z)π/sin(πz) and explicit estimates on square paths.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Distinguish the continuation of a single-valued meromorphic function from the choice of a branch of a multivalued expression.
  • Prove that the gamma integral is analytic for Re⁡z>0\Re z>0Rez>0, continue it with the recurrence, and calculate its residues at the nonpositive integers.
  • Evaluate ∑n∈Zh(n)\sum_{n\in\Z}h(n)∑n∈Z​h(n) and ∑n∈Z(−1)nh(n)\sum_{n\in\Z}(-1)^nh(n)∑n∈Z​(−1)nh(n) by residues for a rational function h=P/Qh=P/Qh=P/Q with deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+2\deg Q\ge\deg P+2degQ≥degP+2 and no zero of QQQ at an integer, and justify the auxiliary function and the estimate on the squares.
  • Recognize when a residue sum fails, for a rational function that decays only like 1/∣z∣1/\abs z1/∣z∣.

Lecture 18 proved that an analytic function on a domain is determined by its values on any set with a limit point in the domain, and that an integral depending on a complex parameter is analytic under a domination condition. In this lecture we use both results to extend the gamma function of GM 27 from the positive real axis to the whole plane except the points 0,−1,−2,…0,-1,-2,\ldots0,−1,−2,…, where it has poles. We then use the residue theorem of Lecture 19 in the opposite direction: instead of evaluating an integral by residues, we evaluate an infinite sum by writing its terms as residues and estimating an integral. The lecture reads in three stages: meromorphic functions and unique continuation (Section 21.1), the gamma function and its continuation (Sections 21.2–21.3), and residue sums (Section 21.4).

21.1 Meromorphic functions and unique continuation

Many functions of this course are analytic except at isolated poles: rational functions, tan⁡z\tan ztanz, and the gamma function below. We give them a name.

Definition 21.1 (Meromorphic function). Let U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C be open. A function fff is meromorphic on UUU if there is a set S⊂US\subset US⊂U with the following properties: each point z∈Uz\in Uz∈U has a disc Br(z)⊂UB_r(z)\subset UBr​(z)⊂U that contains no point of SSS other than possibly zzz itself; fff is analytic on U∖SU\setminus SU∖S; and each point of SSS is a pole of fff.

The first property says that SSS has no limit point in UUU in the sense of Lecture 18: the poles do not accumulate at any point of UUU. It also makes U∖SU\setminus SU∖S open: a point w∈U∖Sw\in U\setminus Sw∈U∖S has a disc Br(w)⊂UB_r(w)\subset UBr​(w)⊂U without points of SSS other than www, and w∉Sw\notin Sw∈/S. By the first property, fff is analytic on a punctured disc about each point of SSS, so every point of SSS is an isolated singular point of fff in the sense of Lecture 18.

A rational function P/QP/QP/Q, with the common zeros of PPP and QQQ cancelled, is meromorphic on C\CC, with SSS the set of zeros of QQQ. To see this, write z=x+iyz=x+\iu yz=x+iy. The definitions of sin⁡\sinsin and cos⁡\coscos through e±iz\ee^{\pm\iu z}e±iz (Lecture 15) give sin⁡z=sin⁡xcosh⁡y+icos⁡xsinh⁡y,cos⁡z=cos⁡xcosh⁡y−isin⁡xsinh⁡y.\sin z=\sin x\cosh y+\iu\cos x\sinh y,\qquad \cos z=\cos x\cosh y-\iu\sin x\sinh y .sinz=sinxcoshy+icosxsinhy,cosz=cosxcoshy−isinxsinhy.(21.1) With cosh⁡2y=1+sinh⁡2y\cosh^2y=1+\sinh^2ycosh2y=1+sinh2y this yields ∣sin⁡z∣2=sin⁡2x+sinh⁡2y,∣cos⁡z∣2=cos⁡2x+sinh⁡2y,\abs{\sin z}^2=\sin^2x+\sinh^2y,\qquad \abs{\cos z}^2=\cos^2x+\sinh^2y ,∣sinz∣2=sin2x+sinh2y,∣cosz∣2=cos2x+sinh2y,(21.2) Hence sin⁡(πz)=0\sin(\pi z)=0sin(πz)=0 exactly when sinh⁡(πy)=0\sinh(\pi y)=0sinh(πy)=0 and sin⁡(πx)=0\sin(\pi x)=0sin(πx)=0, that is, when zzz is an integer. Each integer nnn is a simple zero, because the derivative πcos⁡(πn)=π(−1)n\pi\cos(\pi n)=\pi(-1)^nπcos(πn)=π(−1)n is not 000. By Lecture 18 a quotient g/qg/qg/q with g(n)≠0g(n)\ne0g(n)=0 and a simple zero of qqq at nnn has a simple pole there.

The function e1/z\ee^{1/z}e1/z is not meromorphic on C\CC, because its singularity at 000 is essential (Lecture 18). No function analytic on C∖{0}\C\setminus\{0\}C∖{0} is a logarithm of zzz, by the proposition of Lecture 16 on the absence of a logarithm around the origin. The principal logarithm is analytic on its cut plane, but no function meromorphic near a point x<0x<0x<0 of the cut agrees with it off the cut. Such a function cannot have a pole at xxx, because Log⁡\LogLog is bounded near xxx. It cannot be analytic at xxx, because the two boundary values of Log⁡\LogLog at xxx differ by 2πi2\pi\iu2πi (Lecture 16).

The identity theorem of Lecture 18 applies on a domain, a nonempty open set in which any two points are joined by a polygonal path in the set (Lecture 15). For a meromorphic function the relevant domain is U∖SU\setminus SU∖S, and for the sets of poles in this lecture we check directly that it is a domain.

Lemma 21.2 (The plane minus a set of real points). Let S⊂RS\subset\RS⊂R be a set with S≠RS\ne\RS=R and without limit points in C\CC. Then C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S is a domain.

Proof. The set C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S is open by the remark after Definition 21.1, applied with U=CU=\CU=C. We join every point of C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S to i\iui by a polygonal path in C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S. The upper half-plane Im⁡z>0\Im z>0Imz>0 is convex and contains no point of SSS, so a point there is joined to i\iui by a segment. A real point x∉Sx\notin Sx∈/S is joined to x+ix+\iux+i by a vertical segment, which meets R\RR only at xxx. For the lower half-plane choose x0∈R∖Sx_0\in\R\setminus Sx0​∈R∖S. A point zzz with Im⁡z<0\Im z<0Imz<0 is joined by a segment to x0−ix_0-\iux0​−i, then vertically to x0+ix_0+\iux0​+i through x0x_0x0​, and then to i\iui. ■

The lemma applies to S=ZS=\ZS=Z and to S={0,−1,−2,…}S=\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}S={0,−1,−2,…}. A disc of radius 12\tfrac1221​ about an integer contains no other integer. A point z∉Zz\notin\Zz∈/Z has a nearest integer nnn, and the disc Br(z)B_r(z)Br​(z) with r=∣z−n∣>0r=\abs{z-n}>0r=∣z−n∣>0 contains no integer.

Definition 21.3 (Meromorphic continuation). Let V⊂UV\subset UV⊂U be nonempty open sets, and let fff be analytic on VVV. A meromorphic continuation of fff to UUU is a function FFF meromorphic on UUU, with a set of poles SSS, such that F=fF=fF=f on V∖SV\setminus SV∖S.

Proposition 21.4 (Uniqueness of meromorphic continuation). Let UUU be a domain, and let S⊂US\subset US⊂U be a set without limit points in UUU such that U∖SU\setminus SU∖S is a domain. If two functions analytic on U∖SU\setminus SU∖S agree on a set that has a limit point in U∖SU\setminus SU∖S, then they agree on U∖SU\setminus SU∖S. In particular, a function analytic on a nonempty open set V⊂UV\subset UV⊂U has at most one meromorphic continuation to UUU whose poles lie in SSS.

Proof. First, the difference of two such functions is analytic on the domain U∖SU\setminus SU∖S, and its zeros have a limit point there. By the identity theorem of Lecture 18 the difference is 000 on U∖SU\setminus SU∖S. Next, two meromorphic continuations of fff with poles in SSS are analytic on U∖SU\setminus SU∖S and agree on the nonempty open set V∖SV\setminus SV∖S, every point of which is a limit point of it. By the first statement they agree on U∖SU\setminus SU∖S. ■

Hence a meromorphic function on C\CC whose poles lie in a set SSS as in Lemma 21.2 is determined by its values on any segment or small disc outside SSS.

Continuing a function that is already analytic on the plane minus a set of poles differs from continuing a logarithm along paths. Lecture 16 followed a branch of the logarithm along a path through a chain of discs. We now make this idea precise and prove the uniqueness announced there.

The proposition does not say that a continuation exists. Along a closed path the continuation need not return to its starting function. The next proposition shows that it does return for a function analytic on the plane minus a set of poles.

Proposition 21.7 (Continuation without a choice). Let SSS satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 21.2, and let GGG be analytic on C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S. Then every continuation along a path whose discs VjV_jVj​ lie in C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S, and which starts with a function f1f_1f1​ equal to GGG near the initial point, ends with fN=Gon VN.f_N=G\quad\text{on }V_N .fN​=Gon VN​.

Proof. We argue by induction on jjj. The disc V1V_1V1​ is a domain, and f1=Gf_1=Gf1​=G on a smaller disc, so f1=Gf_1=Gf1​=G on V1V_1V1​ by the identity theorem. If fj=Gf_j=Gfj​=G on VjV_jVj​, then fj+1=fj=Gf_{j+1}=f_j=Gfj+1​=fj​=G on Vj∩Vj+1V_j\cap V_{j+1}Vj​∩Vj+1​, which is a nonempty open set, so fj+1=Gf_{j+1}=Gfj+1​=G on Vj+1V_{j+1}Vj+1​ by the identity theorem. ■

The conclusion holds whatever the path, closed or not. For the logarithm there is no such GGG on C∖{0}\C\setminus\{0\}C∖{0}. Lecture 16 continued the logarithm along the upper and the lower half of the circle ∣z∣=4\abs z=4∣z∣=4, and the two continuations arrived at −4-4−4 with values that differ by 2πi2\pi\iu2πi. So choosing a branch of the logarithm means choosing a cut, and the value depends on that choice. The gamma function below is analytic on C\CC minus its poles, so its continuation involves no choice. Going around a pole changes nothing, and going around a branch point changes the value.

21.3 Continuation of the gamma function

The recurrence, read backwards as Γ(z)=Γ(z+1)/z\Gamma(z)=\Gamma(z+1)/zΓ(z)=Γ(z+1)/z, expresses Γ\GammaΓ at zzz through its value at a point one unit to the right. Applied mmm times, it reaches the half-plane U0U_0U0​ from any point with Re⁡z>−m\Re z>-mRez>−m. Let S={0,−1,−2,…},Um={z∈C:Re⁡z>−m}∖{0,−1,…,−m+1}(m≥1).S=\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\},\qquad U_m=\{z\in\C:\Re z>-m\}\setminus\{0,-1,\ldots,-m+1\}\quad(m\ge1).S={0,−1,−2,…},Um​={z∈C:Rez>−m}∖{0,−1,…,−m+1}(m≥1).

Theorem 21.10 (Continuation of the gamma function). There is a function analytic on C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S that equals Γ\GammaΓ on U0U_0U0​. Written again as Γ\GammaΓ, it satisfies Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z)(z∈C∖S),\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)\qquad(z\in\C\setminus S),Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z)(z∈C∖S),(21.5) and each point −n-n−n with n=0,1,2,…n=0,1,2,\ldotsn=0,1,2,… is a simple pole with Res⁡z=−nΓ=(−1)nn!.\Res_{z=-n}\Gamma=\frac{(-1)^n}{n!} .Resz=−n​Γ=n!(−1)n​.(21.6) In particular, Γ\GammaΓ is meromorphic on C\CC.

No later result of this course depends on the following identity. It is an optional extension, and we cite it.

Theorem 21.12 (Reflection formula · cited). For every z∈C∖Zz\in\C\setminus\Zz∈C∖Z, Γ(z)Γ(1−z)=πsin⁡(πz).\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\frac\pi{\sin(\pi z)} .Γ(z)Γ(1−z)=sin(πz)π​.

The sibling course Real and Complex Analysis proves it in AN 13, in the section "Beta and reflection" (AN writes sss for our zzz), and Beals and Wong prove it as Theorem 2.2.3. For 0<α<10<\alpha<10<α<1, AN 13 writes Γ(α)Γ(1−α)\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(1-\alpha)Γ(α)Γ(1−α) as the beta integral B(α,1−α)B(\alpha,1-\alpha)B(α,1−α), which the substitution t=x/(1+x)t=x/(1+x)t=x/(1+x) turns into the integral ∫0∞xα−1 ⁣dx/(1+x)=π/sin⁡(πα)\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}\dd x/(1+x)=\pi/\sin(\pi\alpha)∫0∞​xα−1dx/(1+x)=π/sin(πα) of Lecture 20. The step to the beta integral changes variables in a double integral over the quarter-plane and exchanges the order of integration. Lecture 22 states the exchange for the improper integrals of this course as its Fubini–Tonelli rule I3, but its rules contain no change of variables for an improper double integral. So this step rests on AN 13, which justifies it by the Fubini–Tonelli theorem and the change-of-variables rule. AN 4 states both rules for Lebesgue integrals and cites them. The identity theorem then extends the formula to C∖Z\C\setminus\ZC∖Z.

At z=12z=\tfrac12z=21​ the formula gives Γ(12)2=π\Gamma(\tfrac12)^2=\piΓ(21​)2=π. It also shows that Γ\GammaΓ has no zeros off the integers, because its right side has none, and Γ(n)=(n−1)!≠0\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!\ne0Γ(n)=(n−1)!=0 at the positive integers.

21.4 Residue sums

The residue theorem turns an integral into a sum of residues. Read in the other direction, it turns a sum into an integral, which can then be estimated. To sum the values h(n)h(n)h(n) of a rational function hhh over the integers, we need an auxiliary function with a simple pole of residue 111 at every integer, so that the residue of the product at nnn is h(n)h(n)h(n). We also need it to stay bounded on a sequence of closed paths that enclose more and more integers.

The function πcot⁡(πz)\pi\cot(\pi z)πcot(πz) has both properties. Its poles are the integers, by Section 21.1, and Lecture 18 found its residue 111 at each of them. For an alternating sum we use π/sin⁡(πz)\pi/\sin(\pi z)π/sin(πz). By the rule Res⁡z=z0g/q=g(z0)/q′(z0)\Res_{z=z_0}g/q=g(z_0)/q'(z_0)Resz=z0​​g/q=g(z0​)/q′(z0​) with g=πg=\pig=π and q=sin⁡(πz)q=\sin(\pi z)q=sin(πz), Res⁡z=nπsin⁡(πz)=ππcos⁡(πn)=(−1)n(n∈Z).\Res_{z=n}\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi z)}=\frac{\pi}{\pi\cos(\pi n)}=(-1)^n\qquad(n\in\Z).Resz=n​sin(πz)π​=πcos(πn)π​=(−1)n(n∈Z). For the paths we take squares whose sides cross the real and the imaginary axis halfway between two integers. For an integer N≥0N\ge0N≥0 let CNC_NCN​ be the boundary of the square {z∈C:∣Re⁡z∣≤N+12, ∣Im⁡z∣≤N+12},\{z\in\C:\abs{\Re z}\le N+\tfrac12,\ \abs{\Im z}\le N+\tfrac12\},{z∈C:∣Rez∣≤N+21​, ∣Imz∣≤N+21​}, traversed counterclockwise (Figure 21.2). It passes through no integer, its length is 4(2N+1)=8(N+12)4(2N+1)=8(N+\tfrac12)4(2N+1)=8(N+21​), and every point zzz on it has ∣z∣≥N+12\abs z\ge N+\tfrac12∣z∣≥N+21​.

Summary

A meromorphic function is analytic except at poles that do not accumulate in its domain. By the identity theorem, a meromorphic continuation to C\CC with its poles in a set of real points without accumulation is unique. A function already analytic on the plane minus such a set continues along every path that avoids the poles without a choice, and a logarithm does not. The gamma integral is analytic on the right half-plane by the lemma on parameter integrals, and the recurrence continues it to a meromorphic function on C\CC. The function πcot⁡(πz)\pi\cot(\pi z)πcot(πz) has residue 111 at every integer and is bounded on the squares CNC_NCN​, independently of NNN. For a rational h=P/Qh=P/Qh=P/Q with deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+2\deg Q\ge\deg P+2degQ≥degP+2 and no zero of QQQ at an integer, the residue theorem on CNC_NCN​ and the cutoff estimate turn ∑n∈Zh(n)\sum_{n\in\Z}h(n)∑n∈Z​h(n) into a finite sum of residues at the zeros of QQQ.

  • Continuation: two continuations along a path that start with the same function near its initial point end with the same function near its endpoint; a meromorphic function on C\CC whose poles lie on the real axis without accumulating is determined by its values near one point; if a function is analytic on all of C\CC minus such a set of poles, every continuation along a path that avoids these poles, starting from that function, ends with it; a branch of the logarithm needs an open set on which the argument is chosen continuously, and a cut is one way to obtain such a set.

  • Gamma: Γ(z)=∫0∞tz−1e−t ⁣dt\Gamma(z)=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}\ee^{-t}\dd tΓ(z)=∫0∞​tz−1e−tdt is analytic for Re⁡z>0\Re z>0Rez>0; Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z)\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z) continues it to C∖{0,−1,−2,…}\C\setminus\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}C∖{0,−1,−2,…}, with Res⁡z=−nΓ=(−1)n/n!\Res_{z=-n}\Gamma=(-1)^n/n!Resz=−n​Γ=(−1)n/n!; for Re⁡z≤0\Re z\le0Rez≤0 the integral does not converge absolutely, and for real z≤0z\le0z≤0 it diverges.

  • Residue sums: for a rational h=P/Qh=P/Qh=P/Q with deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+2\deg Q\ge\deg P+2degQ≥degP+2 and no zero of QQQ at an integer, ∑n∈Zh(n)=−∑jRes⁡z=zj(πcot⁡(πz)h)\sum_{n\in\Z}h(n)=-\sum_j\Res_{z=z_j}(\pi\cot(\pi z)h)∑n∈Z​h(n)=−∑j​Resz=zj​​(πcot(πz)h) and ∑n∈Z(−1)nh(n)=−∑jRes⁡z=zj(πh/sin⁡(πz))\sum_{n\in\Z}(-1)^nh(n)=-\sum_j\Res_{z=z_j}(\pi h/\sin(\pi z))∑n∈Z​(−1)nh(n)=−∑j​Resz=zj​​(πh/sin(πz)); the proof uses ∣cot⁡(πz)∣≤coth⁡(π/2)\abs{\cot(\pi z)}\le\coth(\pi/2)∣cot(πz)∣≤coth(π/2) and ∣1/sin⁡(πz)∣≤1\abs{1/\sin(\pi z)}\le1∣1/sin(πz)∣≤1 on CNC_NCN​.

Lectures 23 and 24 use the residue integrals of Lecture 19 and the sine integral and principal values of Lecture 20. The gamma function returns with the Laplace transforms of Lecture 26.
